## Special topic: SDitH (Syndrome Decoding in the Head) — integration discussion

This meeting featured a guest session with Nicolas Gama and Thibauld Feneuil from the SDitH team, invited to discuss how to collaborate on including SDitH in liboqs following their advancement to NIST signature on-ramp round 3.

### Overview of the liboqs integration model (Bruce)

Bruce presented a brief walkthrough of what algorithm integration into liboqs entails:

**Namespacing.** The standard NIST API exports generic symbols (`crypto_sign_keypair`, `crypto_sign`, `crypto_verify`); liboqs requires each algorithm and each variant/platform-specific implementation to use namespaced symbols to avoid collisions across the many algorithms and backends it hosts.

**Symmetric primitive substitution.** Upstream implementations typically bundle their own SHAKE/SHA-3/AES backends. liboqs provides optimised shared implementations of these, so integrations are expected to support a compile-time flag that redirects symmetric calls to the OQS backends rather than the bundled ones.

**Metadata.** Each integration requires a metadata file describing algorithm properties (name, type, NIST security levels, key/signature sizes, etc.) and build configuration, which drives the copy-from-upstream script's automatic code generation and build-file synthesis.

**The copy-from-upstream workflow.** The preferred integration path is: the upstream repository holds the algorithm code and an OQS-specific patch/metadata; liboqs clones that repository, applies the patch, and synthesises the public API and build configuration from the metadata. This makes future updates (new rounds, bug fixes, security patches) significantly easier and keeps ownership of the implementation clearly with the upstream team.

Basil added that for skSign (which he is integrating), a GitHub Actions workflow tests the integration continuously during upstream development — giving the submission team early visibility into any liboqs compatibility issues, and providing additional test coverage for the upstream implementation.

### SDitH-specific discussion

**Runtime parameter dispatch.** SDitH's current implementation compiles a single static library and dispatches between Category 1, 3, and 5 parameter sets and between CPU feature variants at runtime via a vtable. liboqs normally compiles each parameter-set/platform combination into a separate object that gets linked into the aggregate library. The team discussed options for accommodating this:

- Basil suggested using a common-code facility in liboqs to share the bulk of the implementation across parameter sets, with a thin per-parameter-set wrapper that sets up parameters and pulls in the shared code — similar to how some other integrations handle large shared codebases.
- Rodrigo noted that while liboqs is flexible, the current compilation model makes it difficult to envision a clean mapping without some structural adaptation. The SDitH team expressed openness to this; Nicolas noted that in the worst case they could duplicate files per parameter set (as the original NIST submission did), though both teams agreed this should be avoided.
- Bruce noted that the copy-from-upstream path is preferred but not mandatory; a manual integration is possible, though more burdensome for future updates.

**Symmetric crypto.** SDitH uses AES and, specifically, Rijndael-256 (the same non-standard extension used by MQOM). Bruce noted this is the second algorithm requiring Rijndael-256, making it worth adding to liboqs's shared symmetric crypto library rather than maintaining it per-algorithm. Nicolas confirmed they use standard Rijndael-256 without modification.

**Round 3 submission status.** Nicolas confirmed that the round 3 deadline has just passed and the final version has been submitted to NIST and published in the public repository. Minor revisions may still occur but the structure is stable and integration work can begin now.

**Platform detection.** SDitH performs compile-time CPU feature detection (SSE2, AVX2, etc.); Rodrigo noted this is compatible with how liboqs handles platform detection and should not require changes.

**Random bytes.** The team uses the standard NIST random bytes API, which is the same interface liboqs wraps, so no changes are expected there.

**Michael's note on copy-from-upstream.** Michael emphasised that a key advantage of copy-from-upstream beyond update convenience is security: when a vulnerability is found in liboqs (which often receives security reports before upstream projects), the fix from the upstream repository can flow back in automatically, rather than requiring a manual patch.

### Next steps

Rodrigo shared the existing tracking issue for SDitH inclusion ([issue #2453](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2453)) as the primary coordination point. The SDitH team will begin exploring the copy-from-upstream integration process locally; liboqs team members will be available for questions via GitHub and at weekly status meetings. The SDitH team is welcome to join any Tuesday status meeting to discuss integration progress.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (SDitH team):** Begin exploring the copy-from-upstream integration structure; raise questions and blockers on [issue #2453](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2453).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Bruce / Rodrigo):** Add Rijndael-256 to the liboqs shared symmetric crypto library, given that both MQOM and SDitH require it.
